sections.title: Min stol, mitt bord, mina böcker · my chair, my table, my books
body: Min lägenhet. Mitt rum. Mina böcker. The Swedish example comes first: the owned thing chooses the ending. Use min/din with one en word, mitt/ditt with one ett word, and mina/dina with every plural. Vår and er follow the same three-way pattern. Hans, hennes and deras never change.
Hans nya bil. Min nya jacka. After a possessive, the adjective uses its definite form, but the noun keeps its plain form: bil, not bilen.

examples.fi: Min nyckel ligger i mitt rum bredvid mina böcker.
examples.en: My key is in my room beside my books.
examples.note: nyckel is en; rum is ett; böcker is plural.

examples.fi: Vår bil står vid vårt hus med våra cyklar.
examples.en: Our car is by our house with our bicycles.
examples.note: vår / vårt / våra follows the owned thing.

examples.fi: Hennes jacka, hennes paraply och hennes skor är här.

body: Jag känner mig trött. Hon tvättar sig. A reflexive object points back to the subject: the doer and receiver are the same person. Use mig after jag, dig after du, sig after han/hon/man/de, oss after vi and er after ni.

sections.title: Sin egen eller hans? · his own, or someone else's?
body: Alex tar sin telefon. Alex tar hans telefon. Sin means the subject's own; hans means another man's. First find the subject of this clause. Then ask whether that same person owns the thing. Use sin before an en-word, sitt before an ett-word and sina before a plural. A clause is one small unit with a subject and a verb; check the owner again in each clause.

examples.fi: Alex städar sitt rum och Henrik städar hans kök.
examples.en: Alex cleans his own room, and Henrik cleans his kitchen.
examples.note: sitt points to Alex; hans in the second clause points away from Henrik, here to Alex.

examples.en: The children take their own jackets.

sections.memoryTip: Subject first, owner second. Same person: sin. Different person: hans, hennes or deras.

sections.title: Man tar hand om sina saker · man means people in general
body: Man brukar dricka kaffe i Finland. Man means people in general: one, you, we or people. It does not mean one named man. Its object form is en, and its own things are sin, sitt and sina.

Man vill att ens vänner mår bra. Use ens when the thing belongs to people in general and sin cannot point to the subject of that small sentence: here vänner is the subject of mår. Compare Man hjälper sina vänner, where man is the subject of hjälper.

examples.note: En is the object form; ens can show ownership.

assignment.title: Ownership walk
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Choose one room. Point to six things and say whose they are. Use one en form, one ett form, one plural form, one hans/hennes/deras form and one sin/sitt/sina contrast. Add an opinion with eftersom.

WRITE: Leave your neighbour a 50–90-word message about the missing item.

RETURN: Tomorrow, describe three objects without looking at your notes.
assignment.model: Det här är mitt rum. Min stol står vid fönstret och mina böcker ligger på skrivbordet. Elin har sin väska här, men telefonen är hennes. Alex tar hand om sina saker. Jag tycker om mitt rum eftersom det är lugnt.

takeaways: The owned thing chooses the ending: min stol, mitt bord, mina böcker.
Hans, hennes and deras never change. Sin, sitt and sina point back to the subject of the same clause.
Reflexive verbs point back to the subject: jag känner mig, du känner dig, hon känner sig.
Man means people in general. Use en as object, sin/sitt/sina for its own things in the same clause, and ens when that link is absent.
